name: Vera Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small carpentry crew on building sites, framing interior walls and fitting fire doors. I have a vocational trade certificate, and the younger workers call me over when a frame is out of square. I like watching an apprentice get a hinge right without my hand on the drill; I dislike chasing late deliveries. I use AI now and then to tidy a materials note, then check the quantities myself. My partner and I have grown children, typical pay for the trade, a few months of expenses saved, and some other builders nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that if AI only shortens office forms, the site can carry on. I would still check the door schedule against the actual openings before we order anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our pay and savings can cover a delayed start, and there are other builders within reach. I do wonder whether the foreman will trust a tidy computer list more than the carpenter who measured the wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting doors and have an apprentice check each opening with me before we cut timber. In the first year I would ask the foreman to show the office how our measurements are recorded, then carry on with the same safety checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A short form is fine; an unchecked fire door is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The measured width and the number on the door schedule, side by side. We once had a frame marked standard when the plaster made it narrower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this change retirement plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I still need to see what stopping work would cost, but this mild picture gives us no new reason to rush.

say: **Office forms** may shorten while carpenters still fit and check fire doors.
An **apprentice** should learn the physical measurements.
think: Our **savings** can cover a short delay between sites.
A neat **door schedule** may still disagree with an actual opening.
do: **Keep** fitting fire doors with the usual safety checks.
**Ask** the foreman to show the office how our crew records opening measurements.
S0.quote: A short form is fine; an unchecked fire door is not.
fieldNote: Her **moderate cushion** and some nearby employers soften a minor office change.
She uses **apprenticeship** to keep physical checking skills in the crew while office forms change.

steps.text: Keep fitting fire doors and checking openings with apprentice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office may buy materials and schedule jobs faster, but the carpenters should still sign off fire doors on site. A programme that misses the drying time is no use to anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn a new site schedule if another crew has used it successfully. My own hours might be squeezed if management treats the screen as a promise, though we have some savings and a few other local builders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the digital programme with two completed sites and note delays it leaves out. If an actual funded class place opens on paid time, I would attend in the first year; if our hours are cut, I would apply for posted local carpentry jobs only where the pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the office getting ahead of the walls. If the schedule starts reducing my gang’s paid days, I would be anxious about the household money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which delay would you mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plaster that still feels wet when the schedule says hang a fire door. A fire door fitted before plaster dries can swell and need another paid visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What pay would make another job viable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At least enough weekly hours and wage to meet our regular bills without dipping into savings every month. I would read an actual vacancy before talking about leaving.

say: **Digital programmes** need site checks for safe fire-door work.
Drying time matters more than a neat **office deadline**.
think: My **hours** could shrink if management mistakes a schedule for reality.
A few **local builders** give me options, but wages still have to cover bills.
do: **Compare** the digital programme with two completed jobs.
**Attend** a funded scheduling class if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local carpentry work if hours fall and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible cut in paid days, despite savings and some nearby builders.
S1.quote: A fire door fitted before plaster dries can swell and need another paid visit.
fieldNote: She wants **proof from completed sites** before learning a scheduling tool.
Her **application** is conditional on lost hours and a posted local job with bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Take funded site scheduling class if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local carpentry job if hours fall and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the apprentices that AGI could change the ordering and drawings by 2028, while capable site robots follow around 2031. They still need to know how a fire door closes and seals, not just how to watch a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot that can fit doors might take the last years of earnings I expected. We have several months saved, but I do not want to spend them waiting for a local opening that may never come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our builder for a paid robot-door safety trial and a funded inspection course; a request is all I can make today. If an actual paid-time course place opens, I would complete it, then in the first year after 2028 apply for a posted local door-inspection role only if I qualify and its pay and hours cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the short runway, but I can still do something with the trade I know. A fire door is a bad place to learn by accident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the trial need to test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot would have to fit a door in an uneven opening and show the crew where its fixings sit. A carpenter must be able to stop the work before sign-off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the builder says yes but offers no course place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my carpentry shifts and ask for a date and written paid-time terms. I cannot call a meeting invitation a robot-inspection qualification.

say: **2028 AGI** changes site planning before capable robots arrive around 2031.
Apprentices still need **fire-door judgment** and a stop rule.
think: A **door-fitting robot** could remove earnings I planned to keep.
Several **months saved** would not fund an open-ended job search.
do: **Request** a paid robot-door safety trial and funded course.
**Complete** inspection training only if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local door-inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
S2.quote: I cannot call a meeting invitation a robot-inspection qualification.
fieldNote: Her **trial request** does not claim the builder has offered or run one.
Her **course and application** each have separate conditions: paid place, qualification, local posting and bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Complete funded robot-door inspection course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local door-inspection role if qualified and pay covers bills
Request paid robot-door safety trial testing uneven openings with carpenter stop authority

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the foreman five years is time to test a door-fitting robot on a real building before it reaches every job. With capable robots around 2034, we should agree who signs the fire-safety record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be nearing the end of site work then, but that depends on our household costs and the work still offered. If a safer inspection post pays enough, I would rather move there than draw down savings to stop early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my carpentry role and review retirement costs with my partner each year. If a funded inspection course has an actual paid-time place, I would take it before 2034; in the first year after 2031 I would apply for a posted local inspection post only if qualified and its hours and pay cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious about an income gap, though the longer lead gives me room to check the sums. I want a written job offer, not a promise about future need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who signs the safety record?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified person on the site should verify the door closes, latches and seals before anyone calls it complete. A door-fitting robot’s own report should not be enough to sign off a fire door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figures matter for leaving site work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our regular bills, the income my partner and I can depend on and the savings left after unexpected repairs. We have not decided a retirement date.

say: **2031 AGI** allows real trials before door-fitting robots around 2034.
A qualified person should **sign fire safety** after checking the finished door.
think: My **retirement timing** depends on income and household bills.
A paid **inspection post** is preferable to draining savings for an early exit.
do: **Keep** carpentry work and review retirement costs annually.
**Take** funded inspection training if an actual paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about an income gap, with time to plan.
S3.quote: A door-fitting robot’s own report should not be enough to sign off a fire door.
fieldNote: Her **retirement review** is a budget enquiry, not a decision to leave work.
Her **inspection move** requires a real funded place, qualification and a posted local job at workable pay.

steps.text: Keep carpentry role while reviewing retirement costs annually
Take funded robot-door inspection course if actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection job if qualified and pay covers bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell younger workers a decade is time to learn both hand fitting and machine checks. AGI in 2036 may alter drawings, and capable site robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may have enough income to leave before the robot reaches my job, but I cannot assume that without adding up our costs. If we still need a wage after 2036, I would use the time to move into safe inspection work rather than wait for a machine to take the last site shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid carpentry work and review the household retirement budget with my partner each winter. If we still need earnings after 2036, I would take a funded inspection course only if a real paid-time place opens, and apply for a posted local inspection role only if I qualify and its pay covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but less pressed by the calendar. I want the household budget before I decide whether to hang my last door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you commit to retiring before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have savings, but the amount needed depends on our actual income, bills and health costs. We would choose a date only after working that through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection wage is too low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay in paid carpentry while work is available and check other posted local openings. I would not take a title that leaves our monthly bills uncovered.

say: **2036 AGI** changes drawings before capable site robots around 2039.
Younger workers have time for **hand fitting** and machine checks.
think: Leaving before **2039** depends on real household income and costs.
If we still need **wages**, inspection work may be an option.
do: **Keep** carpentry work and review retirement costs each winter.
**Train** only if earnings remain needed and a funded paid-time place opens.
**Apply** for posted local inspection work if qualified and pay covers bills.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a longer window for household planning.
S4.quote: I want the household budget before I decide whether to hang my last door.
fieldNote: Her **retirement choice** stays conditional on actual costs and income.
Any **post-2036 transition** requires continued wage need, a real paid course place and a posted local bill-covering vacancy.

steps.text: Keep carpentry work while reviewing retirement affordability yearly
Take funded inspection course if earnings needed and actual paid-time place opens
Apply for posted local inspection role if earnings needed, qualified and pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a door-fitting robot could reach the site while I still need years of pay. An actual funded inspection course on paid days, a posted local job at enough pay and a human fire-door sign-off would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: A young carpenter should learn why a fire door closes properly before learning how a robot says it closed. The crew needs to understand the seal, not just read a completion report.

portrait: **Vera Abbott**, 58, leads fire-door carpentry on building sites and holds a vocational trade certificate.
She and her **partner** have grown children, typical wages, several months saved and some nearby building jobs.
She uses **AI occasionally** for simple tasks but wants proven tools and physical door checks before trusting a digital schedule.
She would seek **funded paid training** and a posted local inspection role if robots threaten her remaining earning years.
Her **retirement date** remains open until household income, bills and health costs are known.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives her little time between office change and possible robot door fitting around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A real **funded course place**, a qualifying local inspection opening and human fire-door sign-off would help.
headlineQuote: A young carpenter should learn why a fire door closes properly before learning how a robot says it closed.
